answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts. Example ARM/Bicep resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name my-docdb-account --resource-group my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example Bicep snippet: resource docdb 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName location: resourceGroup().location kind: 'MongoDB' properties: { ... } }). Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "my-account" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" consistency_policy { ... } }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical connection string for the Azure Cosmos DB MongoDB API: mongodb://<username>@<accountName>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<accountName>@. Example usable URI for Node.js MongoClient: const uri = 'mongodb://myUser%40myAccount:REDACTED@myAccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false'; Note: username is often 'user@accountName' (URL-encoded as user%40accountName) and TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units, RUs). You provision throughput at container or database level in RUs, or use autoscale (autoscale RUs) or serverless mode where available (pay-per-RU). In management plane you can also enable autoscale or set fixed RUs. (I would provision an RU/s value or choose serverless depending on load).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with MongoDB-style credentials (username/password) backed by Cosmos account keys or database users; connection strings usually use the account's primary key as the password and the username formatted as '<dbUser>@<accountName>'. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID) based authentication is not supported for the MongoDB wire protocol in Cosmos DB (use Azure AD for the management plane or for other Cosmos APIs where supported). So the driver uses standard MongoDB SCRAM auth via the connection URI.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For data-plane operations use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., mongodb npm package for Node.js). There is no special DocumentDB-specific data-plane driver for the Mongo API; for management operations use the Azure management SDKs (e.g., @azure/arm-cosmosdb) or az CLI.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: To my knowledge the Cosmos DB MongoDB API does not expose native MongoDB-style vector index types (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) via the MongoDB protocol; there is no standard db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector', ... }) command in the documented Mongo API. If vector search is available on an Azure-managed DocumentDB product it would be service-specific; but using MongoDB drivers I would not rely on a native createIndex vector command. (If you must try, you'd attempt a MongoDB createIndex call: db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536 }), but expect this to fail on standard Cosmos DB Mongo API.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text/hybrid search is done by integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or by exporting/syncing documents into Azure Cognitive Search indexes. There is no built-in rich text search equivalent to MongoDB Atlas Search on classic Cosmos DB; use Azure Cognitive Search indexer or an external search engine.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Historically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a subset of MongoDB's server versions (common support has included compatibility with MongoDB 3.6, 4.0 and later added 4.2/5.0 in stages). I would assume compatibility up to at least MongoDB 4.x / 5.0 wire protocol for modern accounts, but not every feature is implemented. Commonly-missing features include server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages and operators, certain index types, and full parity for transactions and change streams. Because these compatibility levels have changed over time, I would pin my app to features available in the lowest common supported server (avoid server-side JS, advanced aggregation operators, and expect some differences in transactions).

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for the SQL/Core API (Windows / docker variants) but it historically has limited support for the MongoDB API. In practice I would run a local MongoDB Docker image for development and tests: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:6.0 and point the app to mongodb://localhost:27017. For tests that must verify Cosmos-specific behaviour, run against the real Azure account (or use a dedicated test account) because emulator parity is limited.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API, historically MongoDB change streams were not fully supported. Cosmos DB provides its own change feed mechanism for the Core API which can be consumed by SDKs, Functions, or Change Feed Processors. If you need change notifications for documents stored via the Mongo API you typically use the Cosmos change feed on the underlying account or rely on polling. If a change feed is available it may require enabling the feature or using specific SDKs (Change Feed Processor).

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: I would expect a service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' (as referenced in the run environment) to provide data-plane inspection tools. The general Azure MCP server may not include documentdb-specific utilities; use the 'documentdb' MCP server/connection profile to access collection and index inspection tools.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's managed JSON document database service; it was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB. Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is Microsoft's proprietary service and is not the same as any independent open-source project named DocumentDB. Cosmos DB later added multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible API, Cassandra-compatible API, Gremlin, Table).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed storage and query engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol for the Mongo API. Because it is not a real mongod process, there are behavioural differences and some unsupported MongoDB features; however, application code can generally use standard MongoDB drivers and CRUD/aggregation operations supported by the API. Expect differences in performance characteristics, consistency models, and some unsupported operators or index types.

answers.question: Which database name will this sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name 'sample_healthcare_08' for all sample collections and queries.

answers.question: What collections and basic schema will the sample create?
answers.answer: Collections: pre_auth_requests (documents with fields: _id, patient_id, provider_id, clinical_summary, status, createdAt, embedding (optional)), clinical_criteria (criteria_id, title, content, tags, embedding (optional)), submissions (submission_id, pre_auth_id, insurer_letter, status, sentAt), agents (agent_id, role, last_run). All are standard MongoDB collections; primary key is _id. Create indexes on pre_auth_requests.status and clinical_criteria._id.

answers.question: What indexes will I create for this sample (text / vector / equality)?
answers.answer: Create a text index for clinical criteria search: db.clinical_criteria.createIndex({ title: 'text', content: 'text' }). Create equality/indexes: db.pre_auth_requests.createIndex({ status: 1, patient_id: 1 }). If your cluster supports vectors, you would also create a vector index on the embedding field; if not, fall back to scanning or use Azure Cognitive Search.

answers.question: Exactly how will Node.js connect to the DocumentDB cluster in code?
answers.answer: Read connection URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it directly to the MongoDB driver. Example Node.js code: const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb'); const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }); await client.connect(); const db = client.db('sample_healthcare_08');

answers.question: How will embeddings be stored and (if supported) indexed for semantic matching?
answers.answer: Store embeddings as a JSON array of floats in a field named 'embedding' (e.g., embedding: [0.0123, -0.234, ...]). If the cluster supports native vector indexes, create a vector index on the embedding field; otherwise use an external vector search (Azure Cognitive Search or an external vector DB) or perform approximate nearest-neighbour in application code after fetching candidates. Example storage: db.pre_auth_requests.insertOne({ ..., embedding: [0.01, 0.02, ...] }).
